title: Evaluating Compositions Involving a Piecewise Function
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Let f(x) = 2 - x and let g(x) be defined piecewise by g(x) = -x for -2 <= x < 0 and g(x) = x - 1 for 0 <= x <= 2. Evaluate: (a) f(g(0)), (b) g(f(3)), (c) g(g(-1)), (d) f(f(2)), (e) g(f(0)), and (f) f(g(1/2)).

steps.title: Evaluate Parts (a) and (b) Using Branch Selection for g
steps.mathExpression: \begin{aligned} \text{(a) } g(0) &= 0 - 1 = -1 \implies f(g(0)) = f(-1) = 2 - (-1) = 3 \\ \text{(b) } f(3) &= 2 - 3 = -1 \implies g(f(3)) = g(-1) = -(-1) = 1 \end{aligned}
steps.explanation: In (a), x = 0 belongs to [0, 2], so use the second branch g(x) = x - 1 to get g(0) = -1, then f(-1) = 3. In (b), f(3) = -1 belongs to [-2, 0), so use the first branch g(x) = -x to get g(-1) = 1.
steps.why: Evaluating a piecewise function requires checking which subinterval contains the input before applying the formula.

steps.title: Evaluate the Self-Compositions in Parts (c) and (d)
steps.mathExpression: \begin{aligned} \text{(c) } g(-1) &= -(-1) = 1 \implies g(g(-1)) = g(1) = 1 - 1 = 0 \\ \text{(d) } f(2) &= 2 - 2 = 0 \implies f(f(2)) = f(0) = 2 - 0 = 2 \end{aligned}
steps.explanation: In (c), x = -1 is in [-2, 0) so g(-1) = 1; then 1 is in [0, 2] so g(1) = 1 - 1 = 0. In (d), applying f(x) = 2 - x twice returns 2 - (2 - 2) = 2.
steps.why: Notice that g(-1) switches from the negative branch [-2, 0) to the non-negative branch [0, 2] on the second application.

steps.title: Evaluate Parts (e) and (f)
steps.mathExpression: \begin{aligned} \text{(e) } f(0) &= 2 - 0 = 2 \implies g(f(0)) = g(2) = 2 - 1 = 1 \\ \text{(f) } g(1/2) &= \frac{1}{2} - 1 = -\frac{1}{2} \implies f(g(1/2)) = f\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = 2 - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{5}{2} \end{aligned}
steps.why: Careful tracking of signs and branch intervals ensures accurate piecewise composition.
